digest.top_line: AREST: adjuvant RT after adequate resection of intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 oral SCC cuts 3yr loco-regional failure 18.9% → 10.6% (HR 0.52), no OS gain.
digest.tldr: Head/neck carried the day: AREST is the first randomised test of adjuvant RT in adequately resected pT1-2N0 oral SCC with intermediate risk factors, and 60Gy/30fx buys loco-regional control without touching DFS or OS, with no toxicity or QoL data in source to price it. Prostate offered process rather than outcome: only 67.0% of high-risk pts got guideline-concordant ADT intent across 26 Michigan centers.

sites.intro: Practice-pattern data, not an efficacy signal: what high-risk pts are actually offered at consult.

studies.name: MROQC ADT Practice Patterns
studies.tldr: 67.0% of 553 high-risk pts got guideline-concordant ADT (≥18mo); ARPI use 23.2% among STAMPEDE-eligible post-publication.
details: 🔍 Prospective statewide quality consortium (MROQC), 26 centers, Jun 2020 to Nov 2024, N=553 intact high-risk M0/N0-1
📊 91.3% recommended any ADT; 67.0% guideline-concordant (intended ≥18mo per 2022 AUA/ASTRO)
📊 27.9% met STAMPEDE M0 criteria; ARPI recommendation rose 0% pre-publication to 23.2% post
📐 Facility-level variability persisted on MVA (mixed-effects, site random intercept), P<.0001
⚠️ Outcome is INTENDED ADT duration at consult, not delivered duration; adherence and early discontinuation unmeasured
⚠️ No outcome endpoint: concordance is measured against guideline text, not against bFFS/MFS/OS in this cohort
⚠️ Michigan-only consortium; generalizability to non-consortium and non-academic practice unproven

verdict.rationale: Prospective practice-pattern survey of intended treatment, no efficacy endpoint. Documents a care-delivery gap rather than testing whether the guideline duration is right.
verdict.audience: Intact high-risk M0/N0-1 prostate ca planned for definitive RT

studies.significance: The deviation is concentrated where the guideline is weakest-anchored: cN1 (OR 2.94) and GG4-5 (OR 6.23 / 9.45) drove ≥18mo recommendations, so the third of pts NOT getting guideline-concordant ADT are largely single-factor high-risk. Facility remained a predictor after case-mix adjustment (P<.0001), which points at practice culture, not patient selection.
studies.monday_clinic: For a man with single-factor high-risk localized disease (GG4-5 or PSA ≥20 alone) heading to definitive RT, this frames how much of the ≥18mo ADT recommendation is guideline versus local habit; it does not address post-prostatectomy salvage or M1 disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective observational analysis within the **Michigan Radiation Oncology Quality Consortium (MROQC)**, a statewide quality collaborative. **26 centers**, accrual **June 2020 to November 2024**, **N=553**. Intended ADT duration and ARPI use were collected prospectively at the treatment decision, not abstracted retrospectively.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Intact (non-postoperative) **high-risk M0/N0-1** prostate cancer planned for definitive radiotherapy. Risk features: cT3/4 **13.3%**, cN1 **19.9%**, GG 4-5 **75.0%**, PSA ≥20 ng/mL **40.0%**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Primary outcome was **intended guideline-concordant ADT (GC-ADT, ≥18 months)** per the 2022 AUA/ASTRO recommendation of 18-36 months. Secondary analyses covered multivariable predictors of GC-ADT, ARPI adoption before versus after STAMPEDE M0 publication, and facility-level variability via a mixed-effects model with treatment site as random intercept.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **91.3%** were recommended ADT and **67.0%** were guideline-concordant. Among the **27.9%** meeting STAMPEDE M0 eligibility, ARPI recommendation went from **0%** pre-publication to **23.2%** after. Site-level variability remained significant on multivariable analysis (**P<.0001**).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The 2022 AUA/ASTRO guideline sets 18-36 months, and STAMPEDE M0 supports ARPI intensification for ≥2 of cT3/T4, GG 4-5, PSA ≥40, or cN1. Both benchmarks are met by a minority here, echoing the long-standing gap between the long-course ADT durations tested in EORTC 22863 and RTOG 9202 era trials and what is actually intended in practice.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intact high-risk M0/N0-1 prostate cancer treated with definitive RT inside a statewide quality consortium. Does not represent post-prostatectomy salvage, node-positive M1 disease, or practices outside a participating quality collaborative.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Intended duration is a proxy for delivered duration, so the true concordance rate could fall further with early discontinuation. STAMPEDE M0 eligibility was applied to a cohort accrued partly before that trial reported, so the 23.2% post-publication figure reflects an adoption curve still in motion rather than a steady state.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The finding that facility explains variance after adjusting for cN1, grade group, and PSA is the load-bearing result: with case mix accounted for, where a man is treated still moves how long he is recommended ADT. That is a quality-improvement target rather than an evidence gap, and it is the kind of signal a consortium is uniquely built to detect and act on.

studies.interpretation:
The useful way to read this is not as a scolding about guideline adherence but as a measurement of where the guideline's authority is actually thin. The 2022 AUA/ASTRO recommendation of 18-36 months treats high-risk localized disease as one bucket, but the odds ratios here show clinicians are not treating it that way: GG5 carried an OR of 9.45 and GG4 an OR of 6.23 for a concordant recommendation, with cN1 at 2.94 and PSA ≥40 at 3.64. In other words, when a man carries the features that also happen to define STAMPEDE M0 eligibility, long-course ADT is recommended nearly reflexively. The third of the cohort not receiving a concordant recommendation is therefore not a random third; it is enriched for single-factor high-risk disease, where the marginal benefit of 18 months over a shorter course has never been isolated in a trial designed to ask that question. Given that 75.0% of this cohort was GG 4-5 and only 13.3% cT3/4, the non-concordant group is likely dominated by men whose only high-risk feature is grade or PSA.

The facility effect is the more uncomfortable result. A mixed-effects model with site as a random intercept still found significant variability at P<.0001 after multivariable adjustment, which means the case-mix explanation is not available. Two men with the same stage, grade, and PSA get different ADT recommendations depending on which of the 26 centers they walk into. That is the classic signature of a quality gap rather than an evidence gap, and it is precisely what a consortium structure exists to surface. It also complicates any attempt to read the 67.0% figure as clinical nuance: genuine individualization would be expected to track patient factors, comorbidity, and preference, not the building.

The ARPI numbers deserve more caution than the headline suggests. Moving from 0% to 23.2% among STAMPEDE M0-eligible patients is a real change in behavior, but the denominator is small (27.9% of 553) and the observation window straddles publication, so the post-publication rate is a point on an adoption curve, not an equilibrium. Comparing it against ADT concordance is somewhat unfair: eighteen months of ADT has been the recommendation for years, while ARPI intensification in M0 disease was new, expensive, and adds a distinct toxicity burden to men who are already going to spend a year and a half hypogonadal. A 23.2% uptake within months of publication is not obviously slow.

The main thing this study cannot tell you is whether the guideline-concordant two thirds did better. Intent was captured prospectively, but no oncologic endpoint is reported, and intended duration is a decision, not a delivered exposure. Real-world discontinuation for cardiometabolic toxicity, fatigue, or patient preference means actual exposure is almost certainly shorter than intended in some fraction of the concordant group, which would push the true concordance rate below 67.0%. For a radiation oncologist, the actionable read is narrow but genuine: the variation lives in your department's habits as much as in your patients, and the single-factor high-risk patient is where your recommendation is most likely to diverge from your colleague's down the hall.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: GC-ADT tracked the features that also define STAMPEDE M0 eligibility (GG4 OR 6.23, GG5 OR 9.45, cN1 OR 2.94), so the non-concordant third is enriched for single-factor high-risk disease. Facility stayed predictive after case-mix adjustment (P<.0001), making department habit, not patient selection, the target.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: ARPI intensification reached only 23.2% of STAMPEDE M0-eligible pts after publication, up from 0%. With 27.9% of this high-risk RT population eligible, the referral and co-management pathway for adding an ARPI to definitive RT plus ADT is the bottleneck, not the evidence.

open_questions: Does intended ADT duration match delivered duration?
Which facility-level factors drive the residual variability?
Optimal ADT duration for single-factor high-risk disease

studies.name: AREST
studies.tldr: 3yr LRFS 89.2% vs 80.9% with adjuvant RT after adequate resection of intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 OSCC; HR 0.52, no OS gain.
details: 🔍 Multicentre open-label phase III from India, N=392 (191 adjuvant RT vs 201 observation)

subdetails: pT1-2, pN0 oral squamous cell carcinoma
Adequate surgery: margins ≥5mm, ipsilateral level I-III dissection, ≥16 nodes
≥1 intermediate risk factor: DOI ≥5 to ≤10mm, PNI, LVE, poor differentiation

details: 🔍 RT 60Gy/30fx over 6 weeks to resected tumour bed and at-risk neck nodal region

details.text: 📊 Per-protocol LRFS and cumulative loco-regional failure (death as competing event)

details: 📊 DFS and OS not significantly different at median f/u 47.2 mo
⚠️ Powered assuming 70% 3yr LRFS in observation arm; observed 80.9%, so event-poor
⚠️ Oral tongue benefit over buccal mucosa is exploratory; subgroup HRs not reported in source
⚠️ No toxicity, xerostomia or QoL data in source; cost of the LRC gain unquantified
🔗 Prior randomised adjuvant HNSCC data (EORTC 22931, RTOG 9501) tested chemoRT vs RT in high-risk disease

verdict.rationale: First randomised test of an indication previously grounded in retrospective data; primary endpoint met, but open-label and the gain is loco-regional only, no DFS or OS.
verdict.audience: pT1-2N0 oral SCC post adequate resection, ≥1 intermediate-risk feature

studies.significance: Transfer hinges on the surgery: benefit was shown only after margins ≥5mm and a ≥16-node level I-III dissection, so a lesser neck operation is not the population studied. Per-protocol the effect strengthens (HR 0.43, 91.1% vs 80.9%), and competing-risk LRF ran 10.6% vs 18.9%. Dose was 60Gy/30fx to bed plus at-risk nodes.
studies.monday_clinic: In an intermediate-risk pT1-2N0 oral tongue resection, this is the first randomised evidence supporting adjuvant RT for loco-regional control, with no survival gain shown; buccal mucosa benefit looked smaller and stays exploratory, and node-positive or close-margin disease sits outside the trial.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Multicentre **open-label phase III RCT** from India, 1:1 randomisation, **N=392** (191 adjuvant RT, 201 observation), stratified by oral cavity subsite, PNI/LVE and differentiation. Median follow-up **47.2 months** (IQR 30-59.4).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **pT1-2, pN0** OSCC after adequate surgery, defined as **clear margins ≥5mm** plus at least ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection yielding **≥16 nodes**. At least one intermediate risk factor required: **DOI ≥5 to ≤10mm, PNI, LVE, or poor differentiation**. Baseline characteristics reported as balanced.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **60Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks** to the resected tumour bed and the at-risk neck nodal region. Technique, target volume detail and dose constraints are not reported in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: loco-regional recurrence-free survival**, from randomisation to first documented local and/or regional recurrence of the index cancer. Kaplan-Meier 3-year point estimates with log-rank comparison; DFS and OS secondary.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary endpoint met on both ITT and per-protocol analysis, and reproduced in the competing-risk analysis. **DFS and OS did not differ** between arms.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The randomised adjuvant evidence in resected head and neck cancer (**EORTC 22931, RTOG 9501**) tested chemoradiation against radiation in high-risk disease defined by positive margins and extranodal extension, leaving the intermediate-risk indication to retrospective series, which the abstract itself names as the basis for the debate. This is the **first randomised test** of that indication in an adequately resected node-negative cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pT1-2 pN0 oral squamous cell carcinoma resected with clear margins ≥5mm and a ≥16-node ipsilateral level I-III dissection, carrying at least one intermediate risk factor. Does not represent node-positive disease, positive or close margins, DOI above 10mm, or a neck staged below that dissection standard.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The observation arm reached **80.9%** 3-year LRFS against the **70%** the sample size assumed, so the trial ran event-poor and the DFS and OS comparisons are underpowered rather than reassuring. No toxicity, xerostomia or quality-of-life data appear in the source, so the price of the local control gain is unquantified. The subsite effect is exploratory.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The whole content of the result is loco-regional control at a median 47.2 months, with no survival separation, so the decision turns on how the reader values preventing a recurrence in a cohort whose failures are visible and often salvageable. The exploratory oral tongue over buccal mucosa split, if it replicates, would narrow the indication rather than extend adjuvant RT to every intermediate-risk resection.

studies.interpretation:
The value here is not the direction of the result, which retrospective series have pointed at for years, but that the question was finally randomised in a population defined tightly enough to interpret. The load-bearing design choice is the definition of adequate surgery: clear margins of at least 5mm and at least an ipsilateral level I-III dissection yielding 16 or more nodes. Much of the retrospective literature on intermediate-risk features is contaminated by inadequate necks and close margins, where an apparent benefit of adjuvant radiotherapy may be salvage of an incomplete operation rather than treatment of occult residual disease. By fixing surgical quality first, this trial isolates the question a radiation oncologist actually faces at the post-operative tumour board.

The most interesting number in the abstract is one the headline graphic does not lead with: the observation arm was assumed at design to reach a 3-year LRFS of 70%, and it reached 80.9%. That gap cuts in two directions. It means this surgical cohort did better than the historical series the indication was built on, which further undercuts the retrospective evidence base. It also means the trial accrued fewer events than it was sized for, so the primary endpoint was met on a thinner event count than planned and the disease-free and overall survival comparisons are correspondingly weak. Reading no survival benefit as a positive finding of equivalence would be a mistake; the honest reading is that this trial was never positioned to detect one.

That leaves a result whose entire content is loco-regional control, and the reader has to decide what that is worth. The competing-risk analysis is the cleaner framing than the Kaplan-Meier estimate, because death is a real competing event in this population, and it puts loco-regional failure at 10.6% with radiation against 18.9% without. The clinical trade is six weeks of radiotherapy to the tumour bed and neck set against that failure rate. What the abstract does not supply is the other half of the trade. There is no toxicity, xerostomia, swallowing or quality-of-life reporting, and in an oral cavity cohort with long expected survival, late RT morbidity is exactly the variable that decides individual cases. Without it the result supports the indication but cannot price it.

The exploratory subsite finding is the part most likely to change how the indication is applied and the part least safe to act on. Oral tongue was reported to derive greater benefit than buccal mucosa, but no subgroup hazard ratios appear in the source, subsite was a stratification factor rather than a powered comparison, and buccal mucosa carries a different failure pattern and a different relationship between depth of invasion and margin adequacy. If it replicates, the indication narrows and buccal patients with a single intermediate feature become reasonable candidates for observation. If it does not, the trial applies as randomised, across intermediate-risk subsites.

For the primary result to be wrong, the observation arm would have to have been surveilled differently or its failures captured differently from the irradiated arm, which an open-label design cannot formally exclude. Loco-regional recurrence in the oral cavity is a hard and visible endpoint, though, which makes that the weakest objection available and the survival question the one genuinely left open.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The target was the resected bed plus at-risk neck at 60Gy/30fx, so this transfers directly to standard post-op practice with no unusual technique requirement. Per-protocol the estimate strengthens to HR 0.43 (91.1% vs 80.9%), so the ITT figure likely understates a completed course. No toxicity data to set against it.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: RT was only tested after margins ≥5mm and a ≥16-node level I-III dissection, so the referral question sits downstream of node yield and margin width. A neck below that bar is outside the evidence entirely, and the features driving the referral (DOI ≥5 to ≤10mm, PNI, LVE, poor differentiation) come off the specimen.

open_questions: Does the oral tongue vs buccal mucosa subsite effect replicate?
Toxicity and QoL cost of the loco-regional control gain
Whether longer follow-up reveals any survival difference

papers.title: Androgen Deprivation Therapy Practice Patterns in High-Risk Prostate Cancer Treated With Definitive Radiotherapy: Prospective Results From a Statewide Quality Consortium
papers.abstract: PURPOSE The 2022 AUA/ASTRO guidelines recommend 18-36 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with definitive radiotherapy for localized, high-risk prostate cancer. The STAMPEDE M0 trial supports intensification with androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) for patients with ≥2 cT3/T4, Grade Group [GG] 4-5, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) ≥40 ng/mL, or cN1. Given advances in imaging, risk stratification, and treatment delivery, we characterized contemporary practice patterns using prospective data from the Michigan Radiation Oncology Quality Consortium (MROQC). METHODS Patients enrolled in MROQC with intact, high-risk M0/N0-1 prostate cancer were included. Clinical information, including intended ADT duration and ARPI use, was prospectively collected. The primary outcome was intended guideline-concordant ADT (GC-ADT, ≥18 months). Multivariable analyses (MVA) assessed associations between clinical factors and GC-ADT recommendations. We compared the adoption of ARPI with standard therapies before and after the publication of STAMPEDE M0. Facility-level variability was evaluated using a mixed-effects model, with the treatment site as a random intercept. RESULTS Between June 2020 and November 2024, 553 patients across 26 centers were included: cT3/4 (13.3%), cN1 (19.9%), GG 4-5 (75.0%), and PSA ≥20 ng/mL (40.0%). Overall, 91.3% were recommended ADT, with 67.0% being guideline-concordant. On MVA, GC-ADT was significantly associated with cN1 (odds ratio [OR], 2.94 [95% CI, 1.44 to 5.99]), GG (GG4 OR, 6.23 [95% CI, 2.85 to 13.62]; GG5 OR, 9.45 [95% CI, 4.46 to 20.06]), and PSA ≥40 (OR, 3.64 [95% CI, 1.22–10.87]). Facility-level variability persisted in the MVA ( P < .0001). Among the 27.9% who met meeting STAMPEDE criteria, ARPI recommendations increased from 0% prepublication to 23.2% afterward. CONCLUSION Within a statewide quality consortium, guideline-concordant ADT recommendations occurred in two thirds of patients, with ARPI intensification in under 25% among STAMPEDE-eligible patients. These findings highlight the need for individualized ADT strategies and collaborative efforts to standardize high-quality care.

papers.title: Adjuvant radiotherapy versus observation following curative surgery for early-stage oral squamous cell carcinoma (AREST; CTRI/2017/07/009114).
authors: AREST Study - Head and Neck Cooperative Oncology Group
papers.abstract: 6000 Background: The role of adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) in early-stage, node-negative oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) with one or more intermediate risk factors - such as depth of invasion (DOI) ≥5 to ≤10mm, perineural invasion (PNI), lymphovascular emboli (LVE), or poor differentiation - remains debatable and is largely based on retrospective data. This multicenter, open-label, phase III randomized controlled trial was designed to assess the impact of post-operative adjuvant RT in this setting. Methods: Patients with early-stage (pT1-T2), node-negative (pN0) OSCC undergoing adequate surgery (defined as clear margins ≥5mm and at least ipsilateral level I-III neck dissection with ≥16 nodes) with presence of one or more intermediate risk factors were screened. Eligible patients underwent stratified randomization (oral cavity subsite, PNI/LVE, and differentiation) in 1:1 ratio to either observation or adjuvant RT (60Gy in 30 fractions over 6-weeks) to the resected tumor-bed and at-risk neck nodal region after written informed consent. Primary endpoint was loco-regional recurrence-free survival (LRFS) measured from randomization to first documented event of local and/or regional recurrence from index cancer. All time-to-event outcomes were computed using Kaplan-Meier (KM) method with log-rank test for comparison and expressed as 3-year point estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The planned sample size (N=392) provided 80% power at an α of 0.05 to detect a Hazard Ratio (HR) of 0.6256, assuming 3-year LRFS of 70% in the observation arm. Results: Following curative surgery, a total of 392 patients were randomized (191 to adjuvant RT; 201 to observation). Baseline characteristics were balanced between the two arms. At a median follow-up of 47.2 months (inter-quartile range=30-59.4 months), 3-year KM estimate of LRFS was 89.2% in adjuvant RT arm vs 80.9% in observation arm (HR=0.52, 95%CI=0.30-0.91; p=0.02) in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population and 91.1% vs 80.9% (HR=0.43, 95%CI=0.23-0.80; p=0.01) on per-protocol (PP) analyses. Cumulative incidence of loco-regional failure with death as competing event was 10.6% (95%CI=6.1%-15.1%) with adjuvant RT and 18.9% (95%CI=13.3%-24.6%) with observation (HR=0.52, 95%CI=0.30-0.91; p=0.021) in the ITT population and 8.7% (95%CI=4.3%-13.1%) vs 18.9% (95%CI=13.3%-24.6%) (HR=0.43, 95%CI=0.23-0.79; p=0.007) on PP analyses. Disease-free and overall survival were not significantly different between the two arms. Subgroup analysis identified oral tongue deriving higher benefit of adjuvant RT compared to buccal mucosa. Conclusions: Adjuvant RT significantly reduces risk of loco-regional recurrence for early-stage, node-negative adequately resected OSCC, particularly oral tongue. However, such reduction in loco-regional failure does not translate into significant survival benefit. Clinical trial information: CTRI/2017/07/009114.
